title: CornerNet: Detecting Objects as Paired Keypoints

problem.summary: One-stage detectors depend on hand-designed anchor boxes: enormous anchor sets are needed to cover boxes densely, only a tiny fraction ever matches ground truth (severe positive/negative imbalance that slows training), and anchor sizes, aspect ratios and matching thresholds add many ad-hoc hyperparameters.
statements: Anchor-based one-stage detectors need huge hand-designed anchor sets (more than 40k in DSSD, more than 100k in RetinaNet).
Only a tiny fraction of anchors overlap ground truth, creating a huge positive/negative imbalance that slows training.
Anchor design introduces many hyperparameters and heuristic choices (sizes, aspect ratios, IoU thresholds).

evidence.quote: But the use of anchor boxes has two drawbacks.
First, we typically need a very large set of anchor boxes, e.g. more than 40k in DSSD (Fu et al., 2017) and more than 100k in RetinaNet (Lin et al., 2017).
As a result, only a tiny fraction of anchor boxes will overlap with ground truth; this creates a huge imbalance between positive and negative anchor boxes and slows down training (Lin et al., 2017).
Second, the use of anchor boxes introduces many hyperparameters and design choices.

background.summary: CornerNet builds on dense one-stage detectors (SSD, RetinaNet) that place anchor boxes over multi-scale feature maps, and on associative embedding from multiperson pose estimation for grouping keypoints; the paper claims anchor-free alternatives (DeNet, PLN) are under-explored.

relatedWork.name: SSD
relatedWork.quote: SSD places anchor boxes densely over feature maps from multiple scales, directly classifies and refines each anchor box.

relatedWork.name: RetinaNet
relatedWork.relation: prior one-stage detector / focal loss source
relatedWork.quote: the authors suggest that the dense anchor boxes create a huge imbalance between positive and negative anchor boxes during training.

relatedWork.name: Associative Embedding (Newell et al., 2017)
relatedWork.relation: grouping technique this work builds on
relatedWork.quote: Our approach is inspired by the associative embedding method proposed by Newell et al. (2017), who detect and group keypoints in the context of multiperson human-pose estimation.

relatedWork.name: DeNet
relatedWork.quote: DeNet (Tychsen-Smith and Petersson, 2017a) is a two-stage detector which generates RoIs without using anchor boxes.

evidence.quote: A common component of state-of-the-art approaches is anchor boxes (Ren et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016), which are boxes of various sizes and aspect ratios that serve as detection candidates.
However, these one-stage detectors are still outperformed by the two-stage detectors until the introduction of RetinaNet (Lin et al., 2017).

solution.summary: CornerNet detects each object as a pair of keypoints: an hourglass network predicts top-left and bottom-right corner heatmaps, per-corner embeddings that group corners of the same instance, and offsets that refine corner locations. A new corner pooling layer looks toward object boundaries so corners lying outside the object can be localized.
solution.approach: Replace anchor boxes by predicting two corner heatmaps grouped via associative embeddings and refined by offsets, with corner pooling extending feature evidence toward object boundaries.
components: top-left and bottom-right corner heatmaps (C channels, no background channel)
associative embeddings with pull and push losses
corner pooling layer on each prediction branch
corner offset prediction with smooth L1 loss
reduced Gaussian penalty for negative locations near positives (object-dependent radius)
hourglass-104 backbone with two prediction modules and intermediate supervision
variant of focal loss for corner heatmaps
soft-NMS post-processing on top-100 corner pairs

evidence.quote: By detecting objects as paired keypoints, we eliminate the need for designing a set of anchor boxes commonly used in prior single-stage detectors.
The embeddings serve to group a pair of corners that belong to the same object—the network is trained to predict similar embeddings for them.
we reduce the penalty given to negative locations within a radius of the positive location.
We use the hourglass network (Newell et al., 2016) as the backbone network of CornerNet.

experiments.summary: CornerNet is trained from scratch with Adam on MS COCO (80k train, 35k train + 5k ablation split of validation) and evaluated on test-dev with single- and multi-scale testing, comparing against one- and two-stage detectors and ablating corner pooling, penalty reduction and the backbone.

evidence.quote: CornerNet achieves a 42.2% AP on MS COCO, outperforming all existing one-stage detectors.
CornerNet achieves an AP of 42.2%, the state of the art among existing one-stage methods and competitive with two-stage methods.
using the ground-truth corner heatmaps alone improves the AP from 38.4% to 73.1%.

limitations.summary: The authors' error analysis shows corner detection is the main bottleneck and grouping errors remain; small-object accuracy lags large-object accuracy, inference is far from real time, and the multi-scale model still trails the best two-stage detector on COCO test-dev.
items: Corner detection is the bottleneck: ground-truth heatmaps alone raise AP from 38.4% to 73.1%.
Grouping errors remain: corners from different objects can receive similar embeddings and be merged.
Small-object AP (19.1 single-scale) is far below large-object AP (54.3) on test-dev.
Average inference time is 244 ms per image (original + flipped fusion), so it is not real time.
Multi-scale CornerNet (42.2 AP) still trails D-RFCN + SNIP (45.7 AP) on test-dev.

evidence.quote: Using the ground-truth heatmaps alone improves the AP from 38.4% to 73.1%, suggesting that the main bottleneck of CornerNet is detecting corners.
The first row shows images where CornerNet mistakenly combines boundary evidence from different objects.

futureDirections.direction: Improve both corner detection and corner grouping, which the error analysis identifies as leaving ample room for improvement.
futureDirections.quote: there is still ample room for improvement in both detecting and grouping corners, the main bottleneck is detecting corners.

equations.name: Focal loss variant
equations.expr: Ldet = -1/N sum alpha(1-p)^beta log(p) if y=1 else alpha(1-y)p^beta log(1-p)

equations.name: Push loss
equations.expr: Lpush = 1/(N(N-1)) sum_k sum_{j!=k} max(0, delta - |e_k - e_j|)

equations.name: Top-left corner pooling
equations.expr: t_ij = max(f_t(i,j), t_(i+1,j)); l_ij = max(f_l(i,j), l_(i,j+1))
